text: dsh-peer-sessions 是面向 DSH Web 配置的会话协作插件，让用户授权的同级对话互相发送消息并查看进度。它通过一个 composition row 注册 /peers、/peer 命令和 peer_send、peer_inbox、peer_progress、peer_list 工具。用户可连接或撤销会话频道，按通知、请求、回复或普通消息交接工作，读取收件箱和对方近期进度；忙碌对话会在当前轮结束后收到消息。适合并行处理相关任务、同步接口变化或让两个独立会话互相答复。代码不要求额外 API key 或外部服务；频道授权记录写入会话日志。

dsh-peer-sessions links approved DSH peer sessions. Commands connect, list, inspect, and revoke channels; tools send messages, read inboxes, and show progress. Messages wait until a busy peer finishes its turn. No API key or external service is needed; grants are recorded in session logs.
想让两个独立的 DSH 会话互相交接任务和进度。
DSH 里并行开的两个对话能不能互相发消息？
我想查看另一个会话最近做到哪一步了。
让 DSH 的两个同级会话在接口变更时互相通知并答复。
Let two independent DSH conversations exchange requests and replies.
I want to check another conversation's recent progress from my current session.
dsh-peer-sessions 的功能「同级会话消息」：模型可用 peer_send 向已连接的对话发送通知、请求、回复或普通消息，并附摘要、正文和可选路径。接收方正在忙时，消息排队到当前轮结束后送达。
dsh-peer-sessions 的功能「频道授权」：用户用 /peer connect <title> 建立频道并选择授权范围，用 /peer revoke 撤销；/peers 查看频道。
dsh-peer-sessions 的功能「收件箱」：模型调用 peer_inbox 可先查看消息摘要，也可按消息 id 读取完整正文；收到的请求和答复状态会显示在列表中。
dsh-peer-sessions 的功能「对方进度」：用户可运行 /peer progress <title>，模型也可调用 peer_progress，查看同一工作区会话的投影摘要和近期进度。
dsh-peer-sessions 使用前须知：频道授权会写入批准方的会话日志；收件箱和待处理消息状态保存在进程内存中，重启后不会保留。（见 lib/grants.js:54-61、lib/store.js:147-174）
另一个 DSH 会话正在忙时，能否把消息排队等它处理？
Can I send a message to a peer session without interrupting its current turn?

dsh-peer-sessions README · dsh-peer-sessions：> Symmetric, user-granted channels between **conversations at the same level** for
> [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) — two sessions you
> drive yourself, talking to each other. **No parent. No child.**

dsh-peer-sessions README · What it is：Two long-lived sessions — say `/srv/orders-api` and `/srv/web-client` —
that both belong to you and neither of which outranks the other. When one changes an API
contract, it tells the other. When the other finishes adapting, it replies.

This is **not** `subagent`. The dividing line:

> **If one side ending means the other should stop too — that's a subagent.
> If both can live on independently — that's a peer.**

dsh-peer-sessions README · What it is：The existing `send_message` / `list_agents` pair is built on parent-owns-child
(`isOwnedBy`). Peer channels have no ownership, so they cannot reuse it.

dsh-peer-sessions README · The hard rule：**The conversation list an agent sees must be a subset of the list a human sees in the
sidebar. An agent must never talk to a conversation the human cannot see.**

The addressable set is derived from the sidebar's own visibility rule
(`sessionVisible` in `dsh-client-ui-workspace`). The two host reads — note the
service name and the return shape, both of which the first draft of this README
got wrong:

dsh-peer-sessions README · The hard rule：Archived, blank placeholder, and subagent sessions are excluded. Delivery re-reads this
list every single time, so archiving a peer revokes reachability immediately — no listener,
no cache.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Interfaces：**Commands you type**

| Command | Effect |
|---|---|
| `/peers` | List channels: peer, grant tier, remaining quota, peer visibility |
| `/peer connect <title> [once\|session]` | Open a channel; the tier choice uses a native option card |
| `/peer revoke <title>` | Close a channel |
| `/peer progress <title>` | Read a peer's projected progress |

**Tools the model calls**

dsh-peer-sessions README · Interfaces：| Tool | Effect |
|---|---|
| `peer_send` | Send a message; without a grant this raises the consent card |
| `peer_inbox` | Read the inbox: one summary line per item, or the full delivered text of one item by id |
| `peer_progress` | Read a peer's projection + summary |
| `peer_list` | Inspect channels and permissions |

dsh-peer-sessions README · Interfaces：**No client code.** Command output renders through the existing chat UI, consent cards
through the existing user-questions UI, and message provenance through the existing
`form: 'relay'` rendering. This package declares no `dsh.client`.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Loop protection：Two conversations answering each other can go on indefinitely, so there are three
ceilings and one timeout notice. All of them are decided BEFORE a delivery happens — a
refused delivery spends no quota and does not advance the chain. Every number below is a
**config field** (see [Configuration](#configuration)); these are the defaults.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Loop protection：| Guard | Limit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Rate per pair | 30 / 60s | Fixed window, held on the channel |
| Total per pair | 200 | Lifetime deliveries on one channel (`once` buys 1) |
| Hop count | 3 | Depth of a causal chain being RELAYED across conversations; two peers chatting normally are not affected |
| Request timeout | `replyWithin` | Announces once on the asking side, and **never resends** |

dsh-peer-sessions README · Loop protection：`replyWithin` on a `request` (e.g. `"15m"`, `"4h"`) is a real deadline: when it passes, the
asking side sees an `Overdue` notice on its next tool call, the receiving side sees
`[timed out · …]` in its listing, and fetching that body adds a `deadline: OVERDUE` line.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Waiting, and how not to：Delivery is idle-first in **both** directions, and the second one is what catches people:

- your message queues behind the peer's current turn — it never interrupts them;
- their reply queues behind **your** current turn, opening a *new* turn rather than
  interrupting the one you are in. A blocking call is atomic, so a reply arriving during a
  long command waits behind it.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Waiting, and how not to：So an agent should never sleep, poll, or hold `wait_agent` open for a peer. It either ends
the turn and is woken by the reply, or — if it must keep working — **pulls** with
`peer_inbox`, which reads the plugin's own inbox: an already-delivered reply is readable
immediately, even though its relay message only enters the transcript on the next turn.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Waiting, and how not to：While a turn is running, an inbound peer message appears in the **queue strip above the
composer**, printed with its full provenance header — text in that box which is not yours
says whose it is. Each item offers edit / delete / **steer into the running turn**, and
`Cmd`/`Ctrl`+`Enter` interjects every queued message. That is the human's escape hatch when a
long step is holding a reply.

dsh-peer-sessions README · A burst is merged, and every message carries its send time：A long task can receive several messages from the same conversation. The Host claims
exactly **one** queued message per turn, so three messages used to mean three turns: the
first turn read a state that the later ones had already replaced, and only found out after
doing the work. Two changes address that:
section: A burst is merged, and every message carries its send time

text:
dsh-peer-sessions README · A burst is merged, and every message carries its send time：- **Every peer message names its send time** (`sent: 2026-10-17T20:01:02+08:00`, local with
  the offset, directly comparable with the time the runtime context prints each turn).
- **While a queued message is still unread, a newer one is folded into it.** The peer's next
  turn reads one ordered batch, with each message's time and an explicit note that later
  entries may revise or supersede earlier ones.
  - **Nothing is dropped.** If the queued message was claimed first, the new message becomes
    its own turn exactly as before; past `mergeMaxChars` the overflow is delivered separately.
  - `silent` deliveries are never merged — they are injected into the next step, where
    replacing in-flight content would be a different thing.
  - The inbox still holds **one entry per message**: merging happens on the delivery side
    only, and `peer_inbox(id)` returns each message's own body.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Configuration：The thresholds are yours to tune, from the plugin's composition row:

```yaml
- id: dsh-peer-sessions
  name: dsh-peer-sessions
  config:
    hopLimit: 5

dsh-peer-sessions README · Configuration：| Field | Default | What it bounds |
|---|---|---|
| `hopLimit` | `3` | How far a chain may be relayed across conversations before it is refused |
| `rateLimit` / `rateWindowMs` | `30` / `60000` | Deliveries one pair may make inside a fixed window |
| `channelBudget` | `200` | Lifetime deliveries on one channel |
| `hopMemoryMs` | `900000` | How long an inbound message keeps counting as "the one being answered" |
| `inboxLimit` | `50` | Inbox items retained per conversation |
| `requestMemory` | `500` | How many request issuers are remembered for the reply-direction check |
| `pendingGraceMs` | `86400000` | How long an unanswered request keeps being reported |
| `maxCandidates` | `8` | Conversations listed before an ambiguous-title refusal summarises |
| `recentTurns` | `3` | Trailing turns `peer_progress` summarises |
| `previewMaxChars` | `200` | Cap on one preview line in `peer_progress` |
| `mergeWhileBusy` | `true` | Fold a newer message into the peer's still-unread queued message |
| `mergeMaxChars` | `12000` | Body cap for one merged message; past it, delivery splits |

dsh-peer-sessions README · Configuration：- **A row's `config` replaces the whole object — it is not merged.** Naming one field is
  fine (the rest come from the schema's declared defaults, and a test pins that), but when
  *layers* override the same row, the later `config` object wins **entirely**. If you set
  these from two places, list every field you want to keep in the later one.
- **Every field has a default.** A field without one would make an omitted `config` a
  validation failure, and a plugin that fails validation is a **warning** at startup, not
  an error: the profile boots with this plugin silently missing. The defaults are the
  values in the table above, so omitting `config` entirely is always safe.
dsh-peer-sessions README · Data and boundaries：**Grants are written into a session log; everything else stays in process memory.**

dsh-peer-sessions README · Data and boundaries：- **Grants are durable (since v1.3.0)**: opening a channel appends one **plugin record** to
  the log of the conversation whose human approved it — `ignorable: true`, type
  `plugin:dsh-peer-sessions/channel`, never model-visible, outside the released event
  vocabulary. A channel therefore survives a dsh restart, a plugin reload, and a
  disable/enable cycle, until `/peer revoke`. Revocation is durable too: the tombstone goes
  to every live end of the pair, and when the granting conversation was cold at that moment
  it is reconciled from that conversation's log on its next load
  (`sessionController.inspect()`, which does not wake anything).
- **The inbox, pending deadlines, hop memory and the rate window remain in process
  memory.** They describe deliveries in flight, and a restart ends that half.
  `peer_inbox(id)`'s promise ("the body stays readable") is therefore bounded by the life
  of the host process, not by the log's life.
- **The grant lives where it was given, not in the peer's log** — the peer's human never saw

dsh-peer-sessions README · Uninstall：```sh
./uninstall.sh
```

It undoes the four install steps, in this order:

| Step | What it removes |
|---|---|
| 1 | the deployed skill `~/.dsh/skills/peer-session/` |
| 2 | the hand-written `insert` row in the profile's `cordis.patch.yml` (backed up first) |
| 3 | the profile dependency (`dsh plugin remove dsh-peer-sessions`) |
| 4 | this package's `node_modules` symlink |

dsh-peer-sessions README · Uninstall：**Restart the profile** afterwards — the plugin stays loaded until the process restarts.
Route-A installs (through the plugin manager) are removed in the manager instead; run this
script only for the route you actually used, and check afterwards:

```sh
grep -c dsh-peer-sessions ~/.dsh/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml   # → 0
```

dsh-peer-sessions README · Installation：**Use one route.** They all activate the same plugin id. Nothing rejects the duplication —
the composer lists the row twice and the loader mounts that id **once, last one wins, with
no warning** (measured on 0.2.0-rc.2; see `MAINTENANCE.md` §一 安装). So the cost is not a
crash but a **silently shadowed row**: whichever copy comes later decides the row's
`config`, which is the kind of thing you discover after an afternoon of wondering why a
setting did nothing.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Route A — as a bundle, from npm or a repository URL：Published on npm as [`dsh-peer-sessions`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-peer-sessions):

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-peer-sessions
```

dsh-peer-sessions README · The other Route A source: a repository URL (git snapshot)：This package declares `dsh.bundle`, so dsh **0.2.0+**'s plugin manager treats it
as a **composition layer**: installing it takes effect by itself, with **no
profile file edited by hand**.

- Desktop: "Manage plugins" → paste the repository URL (or the npm name).
- CLI (except the `desktop` profile — the official CLI refuses plugin management
  for it, so the desktop app must use its own UI):

```sh
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add <repository-url-or-package-name>
```

> package only when `dsh.bundle` is an object; otherwise it refuses with
> `not-a-bundle` and rolls the profile back. Declared here since v1.0.3.

The desktop installs from a **git snapshot**, not your working copy, so each
release needs an update in the manager.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Route B — local clone + `./install.sh`：```sh
./install.sh
```

It does four things: links this package's `node_modules` to the profile's (so
`@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` resolve, on the **same module
instances** the harness already loaded), adds the profile dependency, appends the
composition row, and copies the skill. `link:` installs are live — edit and
restart.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Route B — local clone + `./install.sh`：> `./install.sh` **skips** appending that row when it finds this package is
> already an active bundle of the profile (i.e. installed via Route A), because a
> duplicate row silently shadows the other one (see above).

By hand instead:

```sh
cd ~/.dsh/profiles/web
dsh plugin --profile web add link:/path/to/dsh-peer-sessions
```

Then append to `~/.dsh/profiles/web/cordis.patch.yml`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: dsh-peer-sessions
      name: dsh-peer-sessions
```

dsh-peer-sessions README · Route B — local clone + `./install.sh`：Copy the skill — a **copy**, not a symlink, because the skill provider lists
skill roots with `lstat` semantics and a symlinked directory is never discovered:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.dsh/skills && cp -r skill/peer-session ~/.dsh/skills/
```

Restart the web profile, then check with `/peers`.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Development：```sh
npm run link     # once per machine: links node_modules to the running harness
npm test         # the whole suite; no harness process required
```

The tests exercise the real `@deepseek-ai/dsh-llm` message construction, and the
real `@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-format-v3-to-v4` admission check as an oracle, plus
a fake host context — so every invariant is covered without a running process.

dsh-peer-sessions README · Development：The link is a **prerequisite, not a convenience**: a bare `@deepseek-ai/*`
specifier resolves against the importing file's real path, so on a machine that
never ran `scripts/link-deps.sh` the suite fails at import. The current test count
is whatever `npm test` prints on its last line.
